1.pericope_label: follow after charity — and what the gift of tongues was

schools.summary: Chrysostom builds the whole comment on the verb of pursuit — a man in chase looks at nothing else, and love keeps escaping because we prefer everything to her.

Ellicott argues at length that the gift was not a gift of languages, from the vocabulary, from its never being used to preach to foreigners, and from the description here; Lightfoot argues from plausibility that no Corinthian minister would stand up in Arabic or Armenian; Robertson glosses the verb for understanding as getting the sense rather than the sound.

Calvin reaches for the proverb about preaching to the bare walls, takes the mysteries in a bad sense as dark and involved sayings against Chrysostom, and notes with Ellicott that unknown is not in the original; Gill hears the violence of hunting in the opening verb.

Henry explains why only two gifts are compared — tongues was the more ostentatious and the more fit to gratify pride — and holds that gifts are proper objects of desire only in subordination to grace.
Clarke calls the chapter crowded with difficulties and prefers Lightfoot's solution, that the tongue meant is Hebrew restored to the church.

debates.question: What was the gift of tongues?
positions: Ellicott: not languages at all, but impassioned utterance expressing feeling rather than thought, unintelligible without interpretation
Lightfoot and Clarke: the Hebrew, a dead language restored to the church, in which the scriptures were read as in the synagogue

debates.question: What are the mysteries spoken in the spirit?
positions: Calvin: dark and involved sayings, obscure and of no profit

themes: follow after charity; desire spiritual gifts
he that speaketh in a tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God
in the spirit he speaketh mysteries

3.pericope_label: prophecy edifies the church; tongues edify the speaker

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the contrast as communion with God against communion with the brethren, and notes that Paul applies his word for building up to a single man on his own account, which is unusual and sharpens the antithesis; Lightfoot widens prophecy to cover singing psalms as well as teaching; Robertson glosses the three words of v.3 and the absent article before church.

Calvin defines prophecy as doctrine fitted to edify rather than foretelling, insists that whatever is done in the church must be for the common benefit, and turns the commendation of languages against contemporaries who declaim against them; Gill puts the practical difference in a clause.

Clarke holds that a useful preacher unskilled in learned languages is greater in God's sight than a man with tongues who does not interpret; Wesley limits the self-edification to the most favourable supposition.

themes: he that prophesieth speaketh unto edification, and exhortation, and comfort
he that speaketh in a tongue edifieth himself
greater is he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues

6.pericope_label: the pipe, the harp and the trumpet

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the illustrations distinct — the first about each instrument having its own sound, the second about distinct notes within one instrument; Robertson glosses the rare vocabulary and calls the word for distinct speech a hint for speakers.

Calvin lingers over the trumpet, the Lacedemonians preferring the flute lest the army charge too hotly, and grants with Plato that music has real power over the manners of a state; Gill notes that Paul argues from his own case.

Henry draws out how much is conceded — an apostle with all his furniture could not edify unless he spoke to the capacity of his hearers, and an exposition in such a tongue would itself need expounding.
Clarke says a speech not understood is dissipated in the air and such gifts are good for nothing; Wesley treats the phrase as proverbial for the utter loss of one's labour.

themes: except I shall speak to you by revelation
if the trumpet give an uncertain sound
ye shall speak into the air

10.pericope_label: so many kinds of voices, and none without signification

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that no word in any language can be meaningless, the thought existing first and the word being invented to express it, and sums the three illustrations as one argument that conveying distinct ideas is the test of usefulness; Robertson traces the word for a barbarian to the mimicking of unintelligible sound.

Calvin extends the argument past men to the whole order of nature, every creature having its own cry, and makes the rule that the tongue ought to be an index of the mind — so that a man chattering in an unknown tongue keeps aloof from the church rather than holding fellowship with it; Gill counts the languages of the world at whatever number one likes.
Clarke reads the opening words as introducing an example rather than a count, each tongue having its own articulation and emphasis.

themes: none of them is without signification
I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian
seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church

13.pericope_label: let him pray that he may interpret

schools.summary: Chrysostom is followed by Calvin in taking the spirit here to mean the spiritual gift itself rather than the Holy Spirit or a faculty of the soul.

Ellicott notes that the Greek hints the gift of interpretation will be granted as well as sought, and keeps the fruitlessness in view as fruitlessness towards others, Paul speaking throughout of public worship; Robertson says the alternative is to stop talking in a tongue, and applies the word for unfruitful to an intellect that gets no benefit.

Calvin rules out two older readings of spirit, faces the difficulty that nobody is recorded as speaking by the Spirit in a language unknown to himself, and answers that Paul supposes a case for the sake of argument — from which he draws a doctrine of prayer against praying with the lips only.
Clarke reads the verse through his Hebrew theory, of a man who reads the prophets in the original and must pray to be able to open them to others.

outliers: Calvin objects that it would be absurd for the Spirit to frame a Roman tongue to pronounce Greek words the speaker did not know, as magpies and crows are taught to mimic human voices — so the case must be a supposition.
themes: let him pray that he may interpret
my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful
the gift of interpretation as the remedy

15.pericope_label: I will pray with the spirit and with the understanding also

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the congregational Amen back to the earliest apostolic times and reads the position of the unlearned man as that of a layman; Robertson explains the word as meaning a private person uninitiated in the gift, who will not know when to say Amen at the close of an ecstatic prayer.

Gill catches the rabbinic idiom of the question that opens the passage and reads the answer as refusing to lay the gift aside; he is at pains that the five words carry nothing they were later made to carry.
Henry insists Paul is not forbidding prayer or song under a divine impulse.

Clarke supplies what the Amen was worth to a Jewish hearer and closes the section with Bishop Pearce's key to the chapter, that understanding means the hearer's grasp of what is said and spirit the speaker's own; Wesley glosses praying with the understanding as praying in a rational manner.

themes: I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also
how shall he say Amen at thy giving of thanks?
rather five words with my understanding than ten thousand in an unknown tongue

schools.summary: Chrysostom explains the change of tone and the fitness of the example — children gape after trifles — and shows why wisdom and simplicity each need the other.
Ellicott and Robertson separate the three ages named in the Greek and render the verbs as processes: cease becoming children in intellect, keep on becoming adults.

Calvin sets the quotation in its own context at length, the threat being that men who will not hear God speaking plainly shall hear him in the accents of a foreign army, so that the Corinthians are pursuing as a benefit what God sends as a punishment; Gill shows that the law here means the whole Old Testament.
Henry agrees that tongues as they used them were a token of judgment rather than mercy.

Clarke separates the three words and presses the warning that a blessing may prove a curse; Wesley admires the stroke as oratory and adds that religion was meant to exalt the natural faculties, not destroy them.

outliers: Calvin turns the verse against a use made of Christian simplicity in his own day, since it is easier to govern the uninstructed and Paul plainly wants believers as fully grown in understanding as possible.
themes: in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men
with men of other tongues will I speak unto this people
tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe

schools.summary: Ellicott insists neither scene is of everyone speaking at once but of one gift exclusively cultivated, follows the steps by which the visitor is convicted, and quotes Bengel's inversion — he will confess that you are not mad but that God is in you; Robertson says they will seem a congregation of lunatics and notes that the confession itself is a quotation.

Clarke grants the visitor could hardly think otherwise, and supplies the mechanism of the conviction — the prophets often having the discernment of spirits; Wesley reads something into the change from plural to singular between the two cases.

themes: will they not say that ye are mad?
he is convinced of all, he is judged of all
the secrets of his heart are made manifest

26.pericope_label: let all things be done unto edifying

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the opening question as asking what follows from the whole argument and describes the assembly with each gift uppermost in its owner's mind; Robertson notes the continuous imperative — the man without an interpreter is not to speak in a tongue even once; Lightfoot is cited for a more orderly account of the confusion.

Calvin admires the balance — no gift of God set aside, however small, but ambition kept from usurping the place due to God's glory — and reads the alternative to public speech as private thanksgiving.
Henry allows two readings of the confusion and asks what edification could come of such an uproar.

Clarke is unsatisfied with the orderly account and thinks each man simply wished to put himself forward; Wesley pictures every one gathering a little company about him as in the schools of the philosophers, and infers from the rule that the gift could be exercised at will without a new miracle.

themes: every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine
by two, or at the most by three, and by course
let him keep silence in the church

29.pericope_label: the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets

schools.summary: Ellicott anticipates the excuse that the Spirit overcame them and gives Paul's answer, and describes the mechanics of the interruption when a revelation came suddenly to a man sitting by; Robertson takes the judging as discerning whether what is said is really of the Spirit, and calls it a principle some had forgotten.

Calvin explains why prophecy gets the same allowance as tongues, wants the less skilful kept from crowding out the better qualified, and answers the objection that God's doctrine should be beyond scrutiny — what is permitted is judging by the Spirit whether what is set before them is his word.

Clarke traces the practice of judging to the synagogue and gives the reason for caution, that a man might claim prophecy without being sent; Wesley presses the contrast with heathen priests, whose possession forced them to speak like madmen.

themes: let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge
ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn
God is not the author of confusion, but of peace

schools.summary: Chrysostom explains the sequence — a third disorder after the tongues and the prophesyings — and notes that Paul asks not merely for silence but for subjection.

Ellicott joins the appeal to the practice of all the churches to this rule rather than to what precedes; Robertson takes the difficulty head on rather than resolving it, setting Paul's plain meaning beside the daughters of Philip and the practice of his own day, and ending in a request for patience rather than a ruling.

Calvin argues from incompatibility, teaching being a position of superiority, but enters two large qualifications — that this concerns ordinary service in a settled church, and that the matters treated are things indifferent.
Henry takes the prohibition to cover praying and prophesying alike, and grants that the earlier chapter seems to assume women did both.

Clarke restricts the prohibition to questioning, disputing and fault-finding on the synagogue model, and is explicit that a woman given an influence to teach was to obey it; Wesley enters the same exception in his first clause.

debates.question: What does the silence cover?
positions: Clarke and Wesley: disputing and questioning in the assembly, leaving the earlier chapter and any extraordinary impulse untouched
Henry and Calvin: public speaking generally, teaching being inconsistent with subjection — though Calvin allows a necessity may require it
Robertson declines to draw the line and asks for patience

themes: let your women keep silence in the churches
as also saith the law
let them be under obedience

35.pericope_label: let them ask their husbands at home

schools.summary: Chrysostom answers the objection that they might as well not be present — they are to hear what they ought, and learn the rest at home.
Ellicott reads the provision as a concession about where questions belong rather than a further restriction.
Calvin is careful that it should not shut women out of learning, and notes that Paul does not forbid consulting the prophets where a husband cannot answer.
Henry gives the rebuke its edge — a church that behaved in a manner by itself and would not endure regulation.
Clarke reads the word for shame of the conduct rather than the sex, and takes it as further evidence that the disorderly are in view; Wesley marks only the place and the persons.

themes: if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home
came the word of God out from you?
or came it unto you only?

fidelity.note: The closing sentences of the entry answer Paul's two rhetorical questions in the summary's own voice — that neither can be answered in a way leaving Corinth free to make its own rules, and that the argument returns to the appeal to all the churches with which the section opened. Henry supplies the purpose of the questions and Ellicott the link to the churches; drawing them together into an answer is the summary's.

37.pericope_label: let all things be done decently and in order

schools.summary: Ellicott calls this the clearest statement of Paul's claim to inspiration anywhere, gives both readings of the textual variant in v.38 with equal weight, and applies the closing principle both to outbreaks of fanaticism and to services held in a tongue the people do not understand; Robertson notes who would be quick to resent the sharpness.

Calvin sets the claim in the frame of the chapter — the judging he assigned to the prophets is what he now invites — but cautions that not everyone may advance it, and explains how rules of external order can be called commandments without binding like the laws of worship.
Clarke reads the sentence as self-testing, compresses v.38 into a phrase, and takes the closing words apart, remarking that the manner of doing a thing often gives the act all its use.

debates.question: How should v.38 be read?
positions: if any man be ignorant, let him be ignorant — his opposition need give no further concern
if any man knows not this, he is himself not known — that is, not known of God

themes: the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord
covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues
let all things be done decently and in order
